Our experience includes Python, APIs, databases, machine learning, and data visualization. By combining technical expertise with academic knowledge, we develop innovative and practical solutions to address real-world scientific and technological challenges.
summary:
Odisea Espacial is an educational 3D browser game developed with React and Three.js. Players design, manage, and lead a complete space mission from planning to arrival.

In the 3D hangar, players select the rocket, propulsion, energy, antenna, shielding, and scientific instruments. Each decision changes the mission’s mass, cost, energy, delta-v, and scientific data in real time. These calculations use real principles, including the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation and the inverse-square law for solar energy.

After designing the spacecraft, players complete the launch, orbital insertion, and deployment of an experimental drone network from a mothership. The missions are inspired by published data from LRO, a lunar mission, and Juno, a Jupiter mission.

The game includes a metrics file that classifies each value as real, derived, or estimated. It also sets current technological limits for energy, communications, and radiation. This helps players distinguish real science, calculated values, and fictional educational elements, such as the ASTRION-X mothership and ASTRION-M drones.

Odisea Espacial brings space-mission engineering closer to Spanish-speaking students and the public. Players learn by making decisions and understanding that every kilogram, watt, and meter per second affects mission success. The project aims to inspire scientific careers and provide a free, fun, and transparent educational tool.
details:
Odisea Espacial is an educational 3D browser-based video game, developed in Spanish, that allows players to design, manage, and lead a complete space mission from planning to arrival at their destination.

The project addresses a common challenge: many people interested in space do not have the opportunity to experience the decisions involved in a real space mission. Designing a mission is not only about choosing a destination; it also requires balancing budget, mass, energy, communications, radiation, scientific instruments, and technological limitations.

The game is played in five stages:

  1. 3D Hangar. The player controls an operator who moves through seven stations: rocket, propulsion, energy, antenna, shielding, instruments, and mission identity. Each component changes five resources in real time: mass, cost, energy, delta-v, and scientific data.
  2. Launch and Ascent. The player participates in a precision-based minigame to keep the rocket within the correct range during ascent.
  3. LEOP. During the Launch and Early Orbit Phase, the spacecraft must stabilize, orient itself, deploy its systems, and establish communication with Earth.
  4. Experimental Drone Network. From a mothership in orbit, the player controls the angle and impulse of a drone. The player must consider gravity, trajectory, and available resources to reach the target.
  5. Arrival and Final Report. At the end of the mission, the player receives a report showing the results obtained, the resources used, and whether the scientific objectives were achieved.

The game includes two missions based on published data from LRO, a lunar mission, and Juno, a Jupiter mission. The virtual assistant, IO, guides the player, explains each decision, and helps them understand the consequences of their choices.

A metrics file establishes real technological limits for energy, communications, and radiation. Each value is classified as real, derived, or estimated, allowing players to distinguish between verifiable science, data-based calculations, and fictional elements created for the game.

Benefits

Odisea Espacial allows players to learn by making decisions. Players discover that adding more instruments can generate more data, but also requires more energy and greater communication capacity. Similarly, adding mass may improve the spacecraft, but it may require a larger rocket or more fuel.

The game develops skills such as:

  • Critical thinking and problem-solving
  • Managing limited resources
  • Understanding engineering trade-offs
  • Reading and interpreting technical data
  • Strategic planning
  • Making decisions under constraints
  • Becoming familiar with physics, energy, and space exploration concepts

The game runs directly in the browser without requiring installation. It includes a 2D version for devices without WebGL support, reduced-motion options, keyboard controls, and a mobile-friendly design.

Expected Impact

The expected impact is to bring space-mission engineering closer to Spanish-speaking students, teachers, and the general public. The project aims to inspire interest in science, technology, engineering, mathematics, and space exploration.

It also seeks to provide a free educational tool for classrooms, where teachers can use the game to explain concepts related to physics, budgeting, energy, communications, and decision-making.

Although there are currently no usage measurements, the team could evaluate impact through pre- and post-game surveys, the number of correct decisions, time spent on each mission, and understanding of concepts such as delta-v, mass, energy, and communications.

Tools and Technologies

The project was developed using:

  • JavaScript
  • React 19
  • Vite 6
  • Three.js with React Three Fiber
  • Drei
  • Post-processing
  • HTML
  • CSS
  • Vitest for automated testing
  • ESLint for code quality
  • pnpm/npm
  • Git
  • A Python static server

The project includes 62 automated tests in the latest documented review. Tests were performed in the Edge browser and across several emulated screen sizes: 1366 × 768, 390 × 844, 320 × 568, and 844 × 390. Physical device testing has not yet been conducted.

Why It Is Creative

The project is creative because it combines real science, playable physics, and clearly identified fictional elements.

  • Scientific honesty: The metrics file labels each value as real, derived, or estimated. It also includes an audit of the fictional ASTRION designs, explaining which elements would not be realistic in real life.
  • Imagined extension: The ASTRION-X mothership and the ASTRION-M mini-probe family propose a possible form of networked exploration. The game clarifies that the real LRO and Juno missions did not deploy drones.
  • Playable physics: The trajectory prediction uses the same integrator as the flight simulation, but only displays a short segment that fades away. This requires players to interpret the trajectory and anticipate the result.
  • Resource management: Each launch consumes a drone, battery, and delta-v. There are no free replacements or retries that restore resources, making every decision meaningful.

Factors Considered by the Team

The team considered several factors during development:

  • Rigor and transparency: Sources come from JPL and NSSDCA. Information that could not be verified is marked as “NOT VERIFIED.”
  • Pedagogy: The LRO mission works as a tutorial, backgrounds unlock components, and explanations use simple language.
  • Accessibility and performance: 3D models are loaded lazily, and the game includes a graphics-quality selector.
  • Branding: The current version uses its own badge and does not use the NASA logo.

Current Limitations

The project still has areas that can be improved:

  • No user testing has been conducted on physical devices.
  • The educational impact has not yet been measured through surveys or learning analysis.
  • The game currently includes two main missions and could be expanded with more destinations, instruments, and scenarios.
  • Some elements, such as the mothership and drones, are fictional and must continue to be clearly explained as imagined extensions.
  • Accessibility can be improved through subtitles, alternative controls, visual-impairment support, and additional language options.

In the 3D hangar, players select the rocket, propulsion, energy, antenna, shielding, instruments, and mission identity. Every decision changes the mission’s mass, cost, energy, delta-v, and scientific data in real time.

The game uses real principles, including the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation and the inverse-square law for solar energy. After designing the spacecraft, players complete the launch, LEOP phase, experimental drone deployment, and final arrival.
